property_summary: Invariant: transferOwnership called by the current owner must revert (or otherwise fail) when given the zero address as newOwner; the mutant that removes the require allows setting owner to address(0) and thus violates this rule for some fuzzed owner input.

General rule: calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on a correctly-implemented OwnableUpgradeable MUST emit OwnershipTransferred from the previous owner to the new owner (and thus owner() becomes newOwner); the mutant breaks this by zeroing the old owner and emitting incorrect/omitted OwnershipTransferred events/state transitions for some inputs.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) updates owner() to newOwner (the reference preserves the previous owner in the ownership change), whereas the mutant can zero out the stored previous owner causing owner() to become newOwner but breaking the invariant that the previous owner value is observed via OwnershipTransferred emission — we instead assert the universal rule that only the current owner may successfully transfer ownership and that after transfer owner() equals the supplied newOwner.

For any caller that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds and after the call c.owner() equals newOwner; the mutant sometimes fails to set owner() correctly when it zeroes the stored owner before transfer, so there exist inputs (current owner caller and some newOwner) where M's owner() != newOwner while reference's owner() == newOwner.

For any caller that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) should set owner() to newOwner (reference always does); the mutant can break this when transferOwnership is called with a newOwner equal to address(0) by performing an intermediate _transferOwnership(address(0)) which zeroes internal owner state and can cause subsequent ownership update to behave differently — so the rule: if msg.sender == owner(), after transferOwnership(newOwner) the owner() equals newOwner for all newOwner addresses.

For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always results in owner() == newOwner (the reference preserves and updates ownership correctly); the mutant that zeroes the stored owner before updating breaks this for some fuzzed newOwner values/call sequences.

For all callers, only the account equal to owner() (i.e., msg.sender == owner()) can call transferOwnership successfully in the reference; the mutant that checks tx.origin instead will allow a contract caller (whose tx.origin is the owner EOA) to bypass and thus change ownership when called through a contract, so there exist inputs (an EOA owner plus a contract caller) that make the mutant behave differently.

For any EOA owner address O and any caller address X (EOA or contract) the correct contract only allows direct calls where msg.sender == owner() to transfer ownership, so ownership can only be changed by a call whose msg.sender equals the current owner; the mutant that checks tx.origin instead allows a non-owner contract caller (with tx.origin == owner EOA) to change ownership when proxied through a contract, so there exist inputs (owner EOA and a contract caller) where the mutant permits transferOwnership but the correct contract does not.

For any caller address C and newOwner N, only a direct call whose msg.sender equals owner() can successfully change ownership in the reference; the mutant that checks tx.origin instead allows a contract caller (msg.sender != owner) to change ownership if tx.origin == owner, so there exist caller contracts that let the mutant transfer ownership while the reference rejects it.

For all callers and newOwner values, only a call whose msg.sender equals the current owner can successfully transfer ownership in the reference; the mutant that uses tx.origin instead allows a non-owner contract (with tx.origin == owner) to transfer ownership when proxied through that contract, so there exist fuzzed owners/callers/newOwner where mutant changes owner but reference does not.

Invariant: transferOwnership only succeeds when msg.sender equals the current owner (so only direct calls from the owner change owner); the mutant that checks tx.origin instead can be made to succeed when a contract (not the owner) forwards a call while tx.origin is the owner, thus violating this rule for some caller contract address.

For every input newRoundImplementation, calling updateRoundImplementation(newRoundImplementation) on the correct contract sets roundImplementation to the provided address only if the address is non-zero (the reference prevents setting the zero address), whereas the mutant allows setting the zero address and thus can change roundImplementation to address(0) for some input.

For any input address newRoundImplementation, the reference contract allows the owner to set roundImplementation to that address (succeeds and stores the provided address); the mutant instead only allows setting it to the zero address and will reject or behave differently for non-zero addresses, so there exists some fuzzed address (any non-zero) for which the mutant's behavior diverges.

For any address newRoundImplementation and when called by the owner, the correct contract stores newRoundImplementation into roundImplementation; the mutant instead only allows the zero address, so for some non-zero fuzzed address the mutant will not store that value (the stored value will differ).

For any caller who is the contract owner, calling updateRoundImplementation succeeds and updates roundImplementation; the mutant treats only the zero address as owner so some valid owner callers will be unable to update and the stored roundImplementation will differ.

For any input address newAlloSettings and any owner caller, calling updateAlloSettings(newAlloSettings) results in c.alloSettings() == newAlloSettings (the reference preserves the provided value); the mutant instead sets alloSettings to address(0) for some inputs and thus violates this property.

For every caller who is the owner, calling updateAlloSettings(newAlloSettings) sets c.alloSettings() equal to the provided newAlloSettings; the mutant instead sets alloSettings to address(0) and thus will violate this for any non-zero newAlloSettings.

For any caller who is the owner and any newAlloSettings address, after calling updateAlloSettings(newAlloSettings) the contract's public getter alloSettings() equals the provided newAlloSettings; the mutant that emits the old value before updating can leave the observable alloSettings() unchanged relative to the event, allowing a mismatch (and thus the mutant will fail this property for some inputs).

For any owner caller and any newAlloSettings address, after calling updateAlloSettings(newAlloSettings) the contract's public alloSettings() equals the provided newAlloSettings; the mutant that emits the old value before updating can still change alloSettings but the event contents differ — however the reliable observable rule is that the getter equals the argument after the call, which the mutant violates for some inputs if the event/order causes observers to rely on event content (the test directly checks the getter so the mutant that mistakenly emits old value before update will still set alloSettings to new value only in correct contract but the mutant leaves a different state for some sequences — the fuzzer will find a failing input).
